title: One Name for Every Living Thing

scenes.tts: In Virginia, some people call a vulture a buzzard. In Britain, a buzzard is a kind of hawk. So which bird do they mean? One common name can mean different birds in different places.
scenes.visual: Two lands, one word: a vulture in Virginia, a hawk in Britain, and the question 'which bird?'
scenes.narration: In Virginia, some people call a vulture a buzzard. In Britain, a buzzard is a kind of hawk. So which bird do they mean? One common name can mean different birds in different places.

scenes.tts: Scientists fix this with one name for each kind of living thing. A species is a group of similar-looking organisms that can mate in nature and have young that can also reproduce. This idea works for many organisms that reproduce with sex cells. It does not fit organisms that reproduce without sex, and some different species do sometimes mate in nature. Each species gets a two-part scientific name.
scenes.visual: Species definition builds from three chips; a limits chip; then two-part name label.
scenes.narration: Scientists fix this with one name for each kind of living thing. A species is a group of similar-looking organisms that can mate in nature and have young that can also reproduce. This idea works for many organisms that reproduce with sex cells. It does not fit organisms that reproduce without sex, and some different species do sometimes mate in nature. Each species gets a two-part scientific name.

scenes.tts: The first word of the name is the genus, a small group of closely related species. The second word names one species in that genus. The turkey vulture is Cathartes aura. The black vulture is Coragyps atratus. The genus gets a capital letter. The second word is lowercase. A scientist in Japan who writes Cathartes aura means the same bird you see in Virginia.
scenes.visual: Name bars: genus and species words; vulture names; Japan and Virginia point to one bird.
scenes.narration: The first word of the name is the genus, a small group of closely related species. The second word names one species in that genus. The turkey vulture is Cathartes aura. The black vulture is Coragyps atratus. The genus gets a capital letter. The second word is lowercase. A scientist in Japan who writes Cathartes aura means the same bird you see in Virginia.

scenes.tts: Scientists also sort each species into eight levels, from most general to most specific. They are domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. A domain is the largest group. There are three: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya. Plants and animals are two kingdoms.
scenes.visual: Eight levels step down from most general to most specific; three domains; plants and animals as kingdoms.
scenes.narration: Scientists also sort each species into eight levels, from most general to most specific. They are domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. A domain is the largest group. There are three: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya. Plants and animals are two kingdoms.

scenes.tts: Think of a mailing address. Country, state, city, and street each narrow the search. The levels of classification narrow it too. Organisms that share more levels are grouped more closely. Scientists decide the groups by comparing body parts, what organisms do, and DNA. Names can still change when scientists learn more.
scenes.visual: Mailing address narrows; levels narrow; two pairs, one shares more levels; three kinds of evidence.

scenes.tts: A dichotomous key is a different tool. It names an organism from traits you can see, one two-choice step at a time. It does not show which organisms are related. So how do scientists know they mean the same living thing? They use its scientific name, shared in every country, and its place in the eight levels.
